intro: Fish, plants, and the parts that keep it all running. Stock moves with the season, so call B&M ahead if you're driving out for something specific. Prices aren't listed: B&M would rather tell you real numbers than guesses.

gear.title: Pumps & filtration
items: Pump sized for 1–2× pond turnover per hour
Skimmer: catches leaves before they sink
Replacement media, seals and UV lamps
gear.tip: Mechanical filtration before biological. And when a pump 'dies', check the intake first. It's usually clogged, not broken.

gear.title: Aeration
gear.lead: Oxygen is what kills ponds suddenly.
items: Lake & farm-pond bottom aeration for big water
gear.tip: Warm water holds less oxygen. Aeration matters most overnight and in a heatwave.

gear.title: Food
gear.lead: Feed the water temperature, not the calendar.
items: Growth / colour food for peak summer
gear.tip: Stop feeding once the water is consistently below 50°F. Fish cannot digest what they cannot metabolise.

gear.title: Treatments & testing
gear.lead: Test the water before you treat the fish.
items: Test kit: ammonia, nitrite, nitrate, pH, KH (alkalinity)
gear.tip: Most fish health problems are water problems in disguise. Bring B&M a sample in a clean jam jar and they'll read the numbers with you.

gear.title: Liner & construction
gear.lead: The unglamorous half of every pond that works.
gear.tip: Koi ponds in this climate are built to about 4 ft, with a bare sloped floor and a bottom drain.

gear.title: Netting & predators
gear.lead: Herons are a real problem, not a theoretical one.
items: Depth: 4 ft defeats a wading heron
gear.tip: Net before the leaves fall, not after. Leaves on the bottom become next spring's water problem.

gear.title: Aquatic plants
gear.lead: Grown on site, so they arrive awake.
items: Lotus, if you have the depth
Floaters, for shade and against algae
gear.tip: Ask which are hardy in zone 6 and which to treat as annuals. That decides whether you buy a plant once or every year.

year.what: Open up and clean out before the water passes the mid-50s. Restart filtration. Fish are waking, but their immune systems lag behind the temperature. This is when problems start.
The busiest weeks of the year. Plants go in, fish are stocked, everything grows, including the algae. Expect a green phase while the system balances.
Warm water holds less oxygen. Aeration matters most now, especially overnight and in a heatwave. Watch for string algae and evaporation.
Net before the leaves drop, not after. Switch to a wheat-germ food as the water cools.
Stop feeding once the water is consistently cold. Close down and prepare for ice.
Keep an opening in the ice with a de-icer and an air stone. Don't smash the ice: the shock is what harms fish. Otherwise, leave them alone.

yearNote: Written for USDA zone 6: New Jersey, eastern Pennsylvania, the Hudson Valley, downstate New York and Connecticut. In zone 7, everything happens two to three weeks earlier.

water.why: Fish waste and rotting food. Toxic even at low levels: the first number to check when fish look unwell.
The half-way stage of the nitrogen cycle. Any reading means the filter bacteria are behind.
The end product. Plants and water changes keep it down; high nitrate feeds algae.
Stability matters more than the exact number. Sudden swings stress fish.
The buffer that keeps pH from crashing, often overnight in a heavily planted pond.
Sets feeding, the pond calendar and oxygen levels. Measure the water, not the air.

waterNote: General hobby targets, not veterinary advice. The overwhelming majority of fish health problems are water problems in disguise.

faq.q: Do the fish survive the winter?
faq.a: Yes, in a pond deep enough, with an opening kept in the ice. They go dormant near the bottom. The danger is not cold water: it is a completely sealed surface, where gases build up with nowhere to go.
Both, ideally. The de-icer holds an opening; the air stone keeps gas moving. Set the air stone shallow so it doesn't stir up the warmer water the fish are resting in.

Usually suspended algae feeding on excess nutrients: often too many fish, too much food, or not enough plants. Green water is a symptom, not a disease. Treating it without fixing the cause just resets the clock.

faq.q: How many fish can I keep?
faq.a: Fewer than you want to. Koi grow, and stocking for the fish you have today is how ponds end up overloaded in three years. Ask B&M with your actual dimensions.
For green water, it works. For string algae, it does nothing: different organism, different fix. Know which problem you have first.
Test the water before you treat the fish. Bring B&M a water sample: a clean jar is enough. Reading the numbers together takes ten minutes and saves guessing at treatments.
